newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak trade deficit widens as steel exports wane.
newsitem.headline: Slovak trade deficit widens as steel exports wane.

text.p: The Slovak foreign trade deficit widened in October, spurred by a decline in exports of metal and steel products coupled with a rise in imports of most types of vehicles.
The Slovak Statistical Bureau (SUSR) said on Tuesday the trade gap for the first 10 months of the year widened to 42.52 billion crowns from 37.17 billion crowns for the January- September period.
Slovakia had a trade surplus of 18.79 billion crowns for the first 10 months of 1995.
The country's main export commodities continued to be iron and rolled steel, accounting for 30.9 billion crowns in the 10 month period, but were still down 11.3 percent from a year ago.
SUSR said that imports grew 38.5 percent, year-on-year for the 10 month period, to 266.66 billion crowns, while exports were increased by only 6.1 percent to 224.14 billion crowns.

Imports of fossil fuels and mineral oils totalled about 44 billion crowns, while those for construction of the Mochovce nuclear power plant accounted for another 40.9 billion crowns. Car imports totalled 24.9 billion crowns.
Metal and steel products imports totalled 7.223 billion crowns, while the imports of the airplanes took up 5.855 billion crowns.

"The volume of imports was influenced by higher imports of all sorts of goods, compared with the same period of last year," the SUSR said. "The biggest growth in imports was in the vehicles, aeroplanes and ships," it added.
Car imports increased, year-on-year, by 11.3 billion crowns in January- October, while imports of airplanes increased by 4.95 billion crowns, over the same period last year, SUSR said.

The Czech Republic remained Slovakia's leading trading partner, accounting for 31.2 percent of total exports and 25.5 percent of imports. Germany and Austria followed with a 20.9 and 6.1 percent share of total Slovak exports respectively.
The second and third largest share of Slovakia's imports came from Russia and Germany, accounting for 17.4 and 14.4 percent respectively.
Trade with OECD countries produced a 13.554 billion crown deficit, while the balance with Russia was in deficit 38.536 billion crowns.
Meanwhile, Slovakia had a surplus of 10.870 billion crowns with the Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA) countries.
